1.definition: An early Swahili settlement on Pate Island in the Lamu archipelago, occupied from the eighth century. Its excavation by Mark Horton revealed an unbroken sequence of African village occupation beneath the stone town and mosques, with no foreign-founder layer.
A large early coastal settlement on Zanzibar, already importing pottery and glass by the eighth century — evidence that Indian Ocean trade reached the coast well before any town grew grand.
An island town near Lamu, among the first places on the coast to build in more durable material than mud and thatch, pulling in Persian Gulf ceramics by around 800.

A tradition in which several Swahili ruling families claimed descent from princes of Shiraz in Persia. The colonial era inflated it into a theory that the whole civilization was foreign; the narrative treats it as a claim to be examined, not a fact.
A British archaeologist who ran large excavations at Kilwa Kisiwani through the 1960s. His careful stratigraphy gave Swahili history its first modern, scientific chronology.

A British archaeologist who excavated Shanga through the 1980s. His dig found an unbroken sequence of African village occupation beneath the stone town, demolishing the colonial myth of a foreign-founded coast.

2.definition: The high inland plateau of the deep southern interior whose goldfields fed both Great Zimbabwe and, carried down to the coast, the Indian Ocean gold trade. The gold did not come from the coast itself; it was mined hundreds of miles inland.

Straight, rot-resistant trunks from the coast's tidal mangrove forests, called boriti, shipped north by the hundreds of thousands to roof houses in treeless Arabia and the Persian Gulf — an unglamorous, enormous-volume export that ran for a thousand years.

A tenth-century Persian author whose Book of the Wonders of India collects sea-captains' tales from the Indian Ocean trade — a source for texture and yarn rather than precise geography, and, like the other early witnesses, not himself Swahili.

3.definition: A white finishing render made by burning fresh coral or shell in a kiln to drive off carbon dioxide, slaking the resulting quicklime with water into a putty, and letting it set back into hard carbonate. On the Swahili coast it waterproofed soft coral-rag walls, took fine carving while wet, and shone white as a marker of wealth.

The characteristic Swahili settlement: a small core of coral-rag buildings under white lime — the congregational mosque, family tombs, and merchant houses — embedded in a far larger body of mud-and-thatch housing where most of the African population lived. The stone was always the minority.

An early Swahili town site on Pate Island in the Lamu archipelago at the northern end of the coast. Mark Horton's 1980s excavation found a stratified stack of rebuilt mosques there — timber, then larger timber, then coral — physical proof that Islam grew slowly from inside the community rather than arriving with conquerors.

British archaeologist whose careful 1980s excavation of Shanga read the town from the bottom of the trench upward and showed its deepest layers were African farmers' and traders' settlement, with a mosque sequence growing in place over two centuries. His work is central to demolishing the colonial 'Arab colony' myth.

The single large congregational mosque of a town where the whole male community gathered for the obligatory communal noon prayer and sermon every Friday, as opposed to the small neighborhood mosques used the rest of the week. Every coastal town of any weight had one.

Recognized, mutually accepted traditions of legal reasoning within Sunni Islam — not sects but rival, equally valid systems of case law, each with its own worked-out method for deciding fine points like inheritance shares or when a sale contract is binding. The four main Sunni schools regard one another as legitimate.

Remembered in the chronicles as a Shirazi prince who came by sea around the turn of the millennium and bought Kilwa Kisiwani from a local ruler for enough cloth to encircle the island, founding its ruling line. The Persian-prince framing is the Shirazi tradition dressing a real African dynasty in a borrowed Islamic pedigree.

4.definition: A fee Denmark levied on every ship that passed through the narrow strait into the Baltic Sea — a textbook example of wealth that comes not from making or growing anything but from standing in the one place everything has to pass through and charging it to go by, the same model Kilwa ran on Sofala's gold.

The dynasty that displaced Kilwa's old Shirazi ruling line around 1300, also known from a sultan's title as the Abuʾl-Mawahib dynasty. Unlike the Shirazi house, the Mahdali claimed to be sharifs — descendants of the Prophet through his daughter Fatima — the single most prestigious lineage in the Islamic world.

Descendants of the Prophet Muhammad, claimed in the Mahdali case through his daughter Fatima, the line through which his only surviving descendants ran. To assert sharif status was to claim the single most prestigious lineage anywhere in the Islamic world, outranking any Persian prince.

The Mahdali sultan who presided over Kilwa's fourteenth-century zenith, known with unusual vividness because Ibn Battuta visited his city in 1331 and wrote him up — praised for raids against the unconverted interior, religious learning, and an almost ostentatious generosity to the poor and to visiting holy men.

Curved stone roofs — the dome a rounded cap, the barrel vault a continuous half-cylinder — built of wedge-shaped stones that each lean on their neighbors, turning the roof's downward weight into an outward push absorbed by thick end walls, so no post is needed in the middle. In weak coral and lime it was genuinely hard engineering.

The vast cliff-top palace and warehouse complex at Kilwa Kisiwani, with over a hundred rooms and a stepped bathing pool above the sea, the largest single stone building in sub-Saharan Africa before the Europeans.

A large rectangular walled enclosure at Kilwa standing beside Husuni Kubwa, built in the same single burst of monumental construction. Its purpose is genuinely unsettled — proposed as a fortified market, barracks, caravanserai, or ceremonial space, with no consensus.

British archaeologist whose large excavations at Kilwa in the 1960s set the city's chronology on a modern footing. Where his archaeology agrees with the partisan Kilwa Chronicle the historical ground is firmer; where the chronicle stands alone it is a story a dynasty told about itself.

5.definition: The travel memoir Ibn Battuta dictated near the end of his life, an account of roughly thirty years and 75,000 miles of journeys across Africa, Arabia, India, and China. It is the single richest written window onto the fourteenth-century Swahili coast, but it was set down decades after the fact, from memory, with a storyteller's eye.

The Swahili gold city on an island off southern Tanzania, capital of the Kilwa Sultanate, which cornered the Sofala gold gate and built the largest stone building in sub-Saharan Africa. Ibn Battuta called it one of the most beautiful and well-constructed towns in the world.

A dynasty of Omani origin that ruled Pate, the northern island heavyweight of the Swahili coast. Its rival house chronicle, the Pate Chronicle, is one reason the coast had several disagreeing stories about itself rather than one.
A fertile island off the East African coast, paired with Zanzibar as a medieval Swahili trading center and, like it, a future seat of Omani power on the coast.

The Swahili patrician class: the established merchant lineages who owned the stone houses, held the urban offices, and controlled long-distance trade. A homegrown commercial aristocracy of lineage, property, and credit, bound across the coast by strategic intermarriage rather than by any state.

Glazed ceramic from the kilns of China, carried west across the Indian Ocean. On the Swahili coast whole bowls were set face-out into pillar tombs and mosque mihrabs, a fortune in trade goods spent so it could never be spent again, conspicuous wealth turned into architecture.

The Swahili carved wooden door: a single massive frame and double leaf of hardwood worked over every inch with chains, lotus rosettes, rope, fish, and Quranic phrases, its brass-studded center post announcing a family's standing before a visitor crossed the threshold. Still made by carvers in Lamu and Zanzibar.

Arabic script adapted to write a non-Arabic language. Kiswahili written in Ajami gave the Swahili their inside voice in chronicles and, above all, poetry, the same expedient Persian and Urdu also reached for.

A long Swahili narrative poem in rhymed quatrains, used for epics, sacred history, and moral instruction, sometimes running to thousands of stanzas. With the shorter lyric mashairi it is the high art of the Swahili inside voice.
Shorter Swahili lyric and aphoristic verse, the lighter companion to the long narrative utenzi in the coast's written poetic tradition.

6.definition: A small, poor, militant kingdom on the far western edge of Europe whose captains spent most of a century creeping down the West African coast in search of a sea route to the spices and gold of the East. Its goal was money: cut out every middleman by reaching the source by sea.

The chain of middlemen through which Asian spices reached Europe before the Cape route: spices crossed the Indian Ocean, were taxed through Mamluk Egypt, and were sold on to Europe by Venice at the top of a price ladder every link of which took a cut.

The experienced Indian Ocean navigator Malindi gave da Gama, who guided the fleet from Malindi to Calicut in twenty-three days, handing Portugal the last and hardest leg of the route. Centuries of tradition named him Ahmad ibn Majid, but the careful modern reading is that there is no good evidence it was him and we do not actually know who he was.
The pepper port on the southwestern coast of India that was da Gama's destination, where spices cheap at the source were the prize of the whole century-long Portuguese project to round Africa.

The Swahili gold city, capital of the Kilwa Sultanate, whose wealth had always rested on its lock on the Sofala gold gate. Sacked by Almeida in 1505 and then strangled by the rerouting of the gold, it shrank into a poor tributary town living among its own oversized ruins.

The king's supreme representative in the East, head of the Estado da Índia. Francisco de Almeida was the first, sent out in 1505 with a fleet and orders to secure the coast, which he did by exemplary terror at Kilwa and Mombasa.

Portugal's seaborne empire in the East, run from Goa: not territory but choke points, a network of fortified harbors and gun-armed fleets designed to monopolize the movement of trade by force rather than to own the places it moved between.

The southern port through which the gold of the far interior reached the ocean and the source of Kilwa's whole wealth. In 1505 Portugal built its own fort there and took the gold port directly, rerouting at the source the trade that had fed the Swahili towns for three centuries.

7.definition: Portugal's state-run maritime empire in the Indian Ocean, headquartered at Goa. It made its money not by governing territory but by selling permission to sail and trade, enforcing a pass system from a chain of fortified ports.

The Portuguese trade-license pass. Any ship moving goods on the western Indian Ocean had to buy one and call at a Portuguese customs post; a vessel caught without a cartaz was lawful prey, to be seized or sunk.
A state-licensed raider — a captain operating with his sovereign's blessing but largely on his own initiative and at his own risk, somewhere between an admiral and a privateer.

A mobile, militarized war-band that came up the East African coast around 1587 to 1589, storming towns including Kilwa and Mombasa. Who exactly they were is genuinely unclear; the lurid cannibalism stories come only from hostile Portuguese sources.

A low, thick, earth-backed fortification with angled arrowhead-shaped corner projections (bastions), developed in Renaissance Italy and called the trace italienne. The geometry absorbs cannon fire instead of collapsing and leaves no blind spot where attackers can shelter.
An Italian military engineer who served as the Estado da Índia's chief architect. He designed Fort Jesus at Mombasa to the state-of-the-art bastion-fort specification of the late sixteenth century.

The heir of Mombasa carried to Goa as a boy and raised Christian as Dom Jeronimo Chingulia, then installed by Portugal as a baptized sultan. In 1631 he reverted to Islam, seized Fort Jesus, and massacred its garrison.

The dynastic history of Pate, a powerful town in the Lamu archipelago that Portugal never fully tamed. It survives in several disagreeing versions set down long after the events, used by historians more for narrative shape than reliable chronology, and is the northern coast's rare inside voice for the resistance century.

8.definition: The seafaring society at the southeastern corner of the Arabian Peninsula, on the same Indian Ocean the Swahili had worked for a thousand years. Its merchants and the coast's had been monsoon trading partners since before this book began; in the seventeenth century it became the sea-power that broke Portugal.

The distinct, austere school of Islam dominant in Oman. Its tradition of choosing a religious-political leader (the imam) by consensus of the community's scholars and tribes was the mechanism that elevated the Yarubids to unite a fractured Oman.

A town in the Lamu archipelago up the northern coast. Its loyal sultan and his people were among the Portuguese allies and refugees packed into Fort Jesus during the great siege, sharing the starvation and disease that reduced the garrison.

Omani-appointed governors who, after 1698, sat where the Portuguese captain had sat and collected what the Portuguese captain had collected. They were the instrument of Omani overlordship over the Swahili towns.
The Arabic script adapted to write Kiswahili, used on the coast for centuries before nineteenth-century European missionaries reduced the language to the Latin alphabet.

A smaller, exquisitely preserved Swahili stone town near Kilwa, inscribed together with Kilwa Kisiwani as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981 — coral architecture officially listed as African achievement.

The vast cliff-top palace and warehouse complex at Kilwa Kisiwani, with over a hundred rooms and a stepped bathing pool above the sea, the largest single stone building in sub-Saharan Africa before the Europeans.
